stem_html:
Archivist Nell Sowande describes her catalogue as ______: it lists what the collection holds and, in the same entry, what a folder's label promises but no longer contains.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"idiosyncratic","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"candid"},{"letter":"C","content":"exhaustive","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"provisional","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The colon defines the word. Read it before the choices.
  • Completeness and honesty are different properties. One choice swaps them.
  • Admitting a loss is the whole content of the entry.

Why A is wrong Idiosyncratic would make the practice merely personal, and the passage presents it as a disclosure rather than a quirk.

Why B is right The catalogue records not only holdings but the gap between them and the labels — what “a folder's label promises but no longer contains”. Reporting one's own shortfalls is candour.

Why C is wrong Exhaustive describes how much is listed. The sentence is about a kind of entry, not a quantity, and a catalogue of absences is not more complete for it.

Why D is wrong Provisional would mean the catalogue is subject to revision, which the colon never says. It says the entries admit losses.

stem_html:
Far from settling the question, the survey ______ it: the two regions that had always been treated as one now look as different from each other as either is from the coast.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"restated","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"obscured","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"C","content":"reopened"},{"letter":"D","content":"resolved","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Far from X” requires not-X. One choice is X itself.
  • A new distinction is clarity, not confusion.
  • The colon reports a result, so the verb must name one.

Why A is wrong Restated would mean nothing changed, but the survey produced a finding that changes how the regions relate.

Why B is wrong Obscured would mean the picture got murkier. The survey made a difference visible, which is sharper rather than murkier.

Why C is right “Far from settling the question” demands the opposite of settling, and the colon supplies it: two regions “that had always been treated as one” turn out not to be.

Why D is wrong Resolved is a synonym for settling, which the sentence explicitly rules out.

stem_html:
The committee's report is ______ in its praise: every commendation is followed by a clause naming the condition under which it would not hold.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"lavish","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"insincere","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"C","content":"concise","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"guarded"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Qualification is not dishonesty. One choice makes that leap.
  • The colon measures the manner of the praise, not its amount.
  • A condition attached to praise weakens it without withdrawing it.

Why A is wrong Lavish praise is unrestrained, and every sentence here carries a restraint.

Why B is wrong Insincere charges the committee with not meaning what it says. Stating conditions is the opposite of hiding them.

Why C is wrong Concise describes length. Adding a qualifying clause to every commendation makes the report longer, not shorter.

Why D is right Praise that arrives with its own escape clause is praise held back, and “every commendation is followed by a clause” of that kind is the colon's evidence for it.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2019 essay on urban trees.

The plane trees on the avenue were planted in a single season in 1903, and for eighty years they were the argument for planting in single seasons: uniform height, uniform canopy, one crew and one budget. Then the same fungus reached all of them in the same year, and the avenue was bare from end to end. What had been the strongest case for uniformity became, within eighteen months, the standard illustration of its cost.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "To show how one example came to support the opposite of the conclusion it had long been used to support."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "To argue that plane trees are unusually vulnerable to fungal disease.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "To describe the appearance of the avenue before and after the outbreak.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "To recommend that cities plant a mixture of species along their streets.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A purpose question wants the shape, not the subject.
  • The last sentence usually names the shape.
  • An implication a reader might draw is not a purpose the text states.

Why A is right The text tracks one avenue across a reversal: what “had been the strongest case for uniformity” ends as the illustration of its cost. The purpose is that turn.

Why B is wrong The fungus is the mechanism of the reversal, and the text says nothing about how plane trees compare with other species.

Why C is wrong The appearances are given, but as evidence for the reversal rather than as the point.

Why D is wrong No recommendation is made. The text stops at what the example now shows.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 article about the history of standardized time.

Before 1883, a traveller crossing the United States reset a watch dozens of times, and no one thought of this as disorder. Each town kept the time the sun gave it, and the watch was wrong only in the sense that it belonged somewhere else. What the railways introduced was not accuracy — the sun had been perfectly accurate — but a single answer, so that being wrong became possible for the first time.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It identifies the specific year in which the change took effect.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"B","content":"It restates the distinction the text is drawing so that the paradox in the final clause can land."},{"letter":"C","content":"It concedes a weakness in the railways' position before rejecting it.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"It supplies a technical detail about how solar time was measured.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A function question asks what a part does for the whole.
  • The paradox needs accuracy taken off the table first.
  • Check where the detail in a wrong choice actually sits.

Why A is wrong The year appears in the first sentence, not in the underlined portion.

Why B is right The dash holds the claim that “the sun had been perfectly accurate”, which separates accuracy from agreement and lets the sentence end on being wrong becoming possible.

Why C is wrong It is not a concession to an opposing party; it strengthens the writer's own distinction.

Why D is wrong No method of measurement is described anywhere in the text.

stem_html:
Text 1

Museums that return objects to their communities of origin lose the ability to display them, but they gain something a display cannot provide: a record of how the object is used once it is home. Several returned masks are now danced annually, and the museum's file on them has grown thicker since the return than it did in ninety years of storage.

Text 2

A file that grows is not the same as knowledge that is shared. The communities filling those files did not ask to be studied, and a museum that treats a return as the opening of a new research relationship has kept the part of possession that mattered to it.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 about the growing file?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"By agreeing that returns produce better records and urging more of them.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"By pointing out that ninety years of storage produced no useful information.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"C","content":"By arguing that the growth of the file measures the museum's continued access rather than a benefit to the community."},{"letter":"D","content":"By denying that any museum file on a returned object has grown.","trap":"too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Disagreement about meaning is not disagreement about fact.
  • Text 2 concedes the evidence and reassigns the beneficiary.
  • “Most likely respond” means find the objection actually stated.

Why A is wrong Agreement is the response Text 2 declines to give; it treats the record as the problem.

Why B is wrong Text 2 says nothing about the storage years, and using them to praise returns would be arguing Text 1's case.

Why C is right Text 2 accepts the file and reinterprets it: “a museum that treats a return as the opening of a new research relationship has kept the part of possession that mattered to it”. The growth measures the museum's access.

Why D is wrong Text 2 never disputes the fact. Its objection is to what the fact is taken to show.

stem_html: Soil scientist Hana Brill proposed that the dark earths of a river basin were made deliberately by farmers rather than deposited by seasonal flooding. Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brill's proposal?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The dark earths are far more fertile than the pale soils around them.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"B","content":"The river's floods have deposited sediment across the basin for millennia.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"C","content":"Pottery fragments occur throughout the basin, in both the dark and the pale soils.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"The dark earths occur only in patches that coincide with the footprints of former settlements and stop abruptly at their edges, while the flood plain beyond carries pale soil at the same elevation."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two explanations, so look for the finding only one survives.
  • Elevation is the control that rules out flooding.
  • A fact true of both hypotheses supports neither.

Why A is wrong Fertility says nothing about origin. Flood silt is fertile too.

Why B is wrong This supports the rival explanation rather than Brill's.

Why C is wrong Pottery in both soils shows people were present everywhere, which is exactly the pattern that fails to distinguish the two accounts.

Why D is right Flooding follows elevation, so a soil that stops at settlement edges while the flood plain at the same elevation stays pale cannot have been laid down by the flood. That is what separates the claim that the dark earths “were made deliberately by farmers rather than deposited by seasonal flooding”.

stem_html: A researcher studying a songbird claimed that its alarm call encodes the size of a predator rather than merely its presence. Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researcher's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The number of notes in the call varied consistently with the wingspan of the model hawk presented, and birds hearing a recorded many-note call fled to dense cover while those hearing a few-note call merely froze."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Birds called more loudly when a hawk was closer than when it was far away.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Birds gave the alarm call whenever any hawk appeared and never otherwise.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Birds of a related species gave a similar call in the presence of hawks.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Encodes X” needs a signal that varies with X.
  • Receivers must respond differently, or the variation carries nothing.
  • Distance is not size.

Why A is right The claim is that the call “encodes the size of a predator rather than merely its presence”, which requires a feature of the call to track a feature of the predator and listeners to act on it. Note count tracks wingspan, and the two calls produce different escape behaviour.

Why B is wrong Loudness with distance is about proximity, not size, and the claim is that the call encodes size.

Why C is wrong Reliable calling shows presence and nothing more — the very reading the claim is set against.

Why D is wrong Another species' behaviour says nothing about what this call carries.

A team compared four storage methods for seed viability. They concluded that freezing preserved viability better than cooling at every duration tested, and that the advantage widened as storage lengthened.

Storage1 year5 years10 years
Room temperature71%22%4%
Cooled (4°C)88%64%39%
Frozen (−20°C)93%85%78%
Dried and cooled90%71%52%

Which choice best describes data from the table that support the team's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Dried and cooled seeds outperformed cooled seeds at every duration.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"B","content":"Frozen seeds outperformed cooled seeds by 5 percentage points at 1 year, 21 at 5 years, and 39 at 10 years."},{"letter":"C","content":"Frozen seeds retained 78% viability at 10 years, the highest figure in that column.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"Seeds at room temperature fell from 71% to 4% over ten years.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A two-part conclusion needs a two-part reading of the table.
  • “Widened” is a trend, so one row of one column cannot show it.
  • Check which two rows the claim actually names.

Why A is wrong This compares the wrong pair; the conclusion is about freezing against cooling.

Why B is right The conclusion has two parts — that freezing “preserved viability better than cooling at every duration tested”, and that the margin widened — and only a comparison at all three durations shows both. 5, 21 and 39 is a widening gap.

Why C is wrong One figure at one duration shows freezing is best at ten years and says nothing about whether the gap widened.

Why D is wrong Room temperature is not one of the two methods being compared.

stem_html: In her novel The Long Field, Aoife Ruane presents her narrator's memory as something she edits rather than consults, so that each retelling of an event differs from the last in ways the narrator does not acknowledge. Which quotation from a fictional novel would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"“Memory, I have come to believe, is less a record than a workshop, and mine has been busy.”","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"“My sister remembers rain; I remember sun; one of us is wrong and neither will say which.”","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"“It was raining, as I have said before, though earlier I had the sun on the gate and the dog asleep in it, and both are true, and I have never told it any other way.”"},{"letter":"D","content":"“I cannot remember whether it rained that day, and I have stopped pretending that I can.”","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Illustrate means enact, not assert.
  • The unacknowledged part is the hard half.
  • Two people disagreeing is a different phenomenon.

Why A is wrong This states the idea as a maxim rather than illustrating it in a retelling.

Why B is wrong The disagreement is between two people; the claim is about one narrator across two tellings.

Why C is right The account has changed — rain now, sun before — and the narrator closes by insisting she has never told it any other way. That is editing “in ways the narrator does not acknowledge”.

Why D is wrong This narrator acknowledges the gap, which is the opposite of the claim.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2020 article about lichens.

A lichen was long described as a fungus farming an alga, an arrangement in which one partner was clearly in charge. Genetic work has since found a second fungus in most lichens, present in every specimen of some species and absent from none, and it belongs to a group unrelated to the first. Whatever a lichen is, it is not two organisms with a landlord.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Lichens contain a fungus, an alga, and a second fungus from an unrelated group.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"Genetic methods have become the standard tool for studying lichens.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"The second fungus is the true controlling partner in a lichen.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"D","content":"New genetic evidence has undermined the long-standing account of a lichen as a partnership of two organisms with one in charge."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Main idea is the claim, not the finding under it.
  • The last sentence is negative, so the answer should be too.
  • Replacing one hierarchy with another goes past the text.

Why A is wrong This is the finding, which is the evidence rather than the point it is used to make.

Why B is wrong Method is the means here, and the text makes no claim about how lichen research is generally done.

Why C is wrong The text unseats the landlord; it does not install a new one.

Why D is right The passage sets up the old account and then breaks it, closing on the claim that a lichen “is not two organisms with a landlord”.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2018 essay on translation.

The translator's difficulty with the poem was not its images, which move between languages intact, nor its metre, which can be approximated. It was a particle that the original attaches to a verb to mark that the speaker did not witness what she reports. English has no such particle, and every workaround — a clause, an adverb, a footnote — converts a grammatical fact into a statement, which the poem never makes.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The hardest element to translate is one the original expresses through grammar, because rendering it in English turns it into an assertion."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Images and metre are the two features translators most often struggle with.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "English is a less expressive language than the poem's original.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The translator should have used a footnote to explain the particle.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two features are dismissed before the subject arrives.
  • The cost is a change of category, grammar to assertion.
  • A rejected option cannot be the recommendation.

Why A is right The passage clears away images and metre to isolate the particle, then names the cost: every workaround “converts a grammatical fact into a statement”.

Why B is wrong The text names both as the things that are not the difficulty.

Why C is wrong One missing particle is not a verdict on a whole language.

Why D is wrong The footnote appears in the list of workarounds the text rejects.

stem_html:
A city replaced the bulbs in half its streetlights with a warmer, dimmer type and left the other half unchanged. Over the following year, reported night-time collisions fell on the relit streets and rose slightly on the unchanged ones, while measured traffic volume fell on both by the same proportion. Because the two groups of streets saw the same drop in traffic, the difference in collisions ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"means the city should relight every street in the same way.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"cannot be explained by the change in how much traffic the streets carried."},{"letter":"C","content":"shows that warmer light makes drivers more careful than cooler light does.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"D","content":"was probably caused by a reporting error on the unchanged streets.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A shared cause cannot produce a difference.
  • The inference is about what is ruled out, not what is proved.
  • Naming a mechanism goes beyond the comparison.

Why A is wrong A policy recommendation needs costs and alternatives the passage never gives.

Why B is right A factor that moved identically in both groups cannot account for a difference between them, and the passage says “the two groups of streets saw the same drop in traffic”.

Why C is wrong The data show an association with relighting, not a mechanism in drivers' attention.

Why D is wrong Nothing in the passage points to a fault in the reporting.

stem_html:
Two colonies of the same ant species were offered identical foraging trails. The colony from a region with frequent flooding abandoned a trail after a single disturbance, while the colony from a stable region continued using a trail through several disturbances before abandoning it. Both colonies were reared in the laboratory from eggs and had never encountered flooding. This suggests that the difference in how quickly a trail is abandoned ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"makes the flood-region colony the more successful forager.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"is caused by differences in the size of the two colonies.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"is inherited rather than learned from experience of flooding."},{"letter":"D","content":"disappears once ants are reared in a laboratory.","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Rearing history is the control.
  • If experience is removed and the difference stays, experience is not the cause.
  • Do not rank the two behaviours; the passage does not.

Why A is wrong Success is not measured. Abandoning early is a cost as well as a safeguard.

Why B is wrong Colony size is never mentioned and the trails were identical.

Why C is right The behaviour differs even though “both colonies were reared in the laboratory from eggs” with no flooding, so experience cannot be the source and origin remains.

Why D is wrong The difference persisted in the laboratory; that is the finding.

stem_html:
The kiln reached temperature four hours later than the schedule allowed ______ potters had already loaded the second shelf, and nothing could be moved.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":", the","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":" the","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"C","content":", and the","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"; the"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Count the independent clauses first.
  • Comma alone between two of them is always wrong.
  • Watch for a conjunction already in the second half.

Why A is wrong A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice.

Why B is wrong With no punctuation at all the two clauses run together.

Why C is wrong The coordinator is available in principle, but the second half already carries its own “and nothing could be moved”, and a second and leaves the sentence with two coordinations at the same level and no clear grouping.

Why D is right Both halves are independent clauses, and a semicolon is the punctuation that joins two of them without a conjunction.

stem_html:
Marine geologist Sena Oduya, whose survey of the trench produced the first complete bathymetric map of its eastern wall ______ that the wall is not a single scarp but a stack of at least four.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", showed"}, {"letter": "B", "content": " showed", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": ", shows,", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "; showed", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A pair of commas is a pair. Find the opening one.
  • Never put a comma between a verb and its object.
  • A semicolon needs two complete sentences.

Why A is right The nonrestrictive relative clause opened with a comma after Oduya and has to be closed with one before the main verb.

Why B is wrong Without the closing comma the interruption is left open and the subject never rejoins its verb.

Why C is wrong A comma after the verb separates it from its own object clause.

Why D is wrong A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and the words before it are only a subject with a modifier.

stem_html:
The three instruments the expedition carried — a magnetometer, a gravimeter, and a seismograph ______ were calibrated on the ship and never opened again until the ice camp was built.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":" —,","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":" —;","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"C","content":" —"},{"letter":"D","content":",","trap":"modifier-attachment"}]

Traps in this question

  • Enclosing marks come in matched pairs.
  • Dashes are used here because the list already has commas.

stem_html:
Neither the two curators nor the registrar ______ able to explain how the crate had been logged twice.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"were","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"B","content":"have been","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"C","content":"are","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"D","content":"was"}]

stem_html:
Having been sealed in the tomb for two thousand years ______ when the chamber was opened.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the pigments began to fade within hours"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "archaeologists watched the pigments fade within hours", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the fading of the pigments took only hours", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "it took only hours for the pigments to fade", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}]

Traps in this question

  • An opening participle attaches to the subject that follows it.
  • Read the subject first, then ask whether it did the participle.

Why A is right The opening participial phrase describes whatever the subject is, and only the pigments were sealed in the tomb.

Why B is wrong This makes the archaeologists the ones sealed in the tomb for two thousand years.

Why C is wrong The subject is the fading, and a fading was not sealed in a tomb.

Why D is wrong The subject is the empty it, which cannot have been sealed anywhere.

stem_html:
The library's reading room, along with its two adjoining galleries, ______ closed for the duration of the survey.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"were","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"B","content":"is"},{"letter":"C","content":"are","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"D","content":"have been","trap":"distant-antecedent"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Along with, as well as, together with — none of these make a plural subject.
  • Strike the phrase between the commas and reread.

Why A is wrong Plural and past, where the closure is described as current.

Why B is right Along with introduces a modifying phrase, not a compound subject, so the verb agrees with the singular reading room.

stem_html:
The committee asked that every proposal ______ accompanied by a budget before the March meeting.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"was","trap":"vocab-collocation"},{"letter":"B","content":"will be","trap":"vocab-collocation"},{"letter":"C","content":"be"},{"letter":"D","content":"is","trap":"vocab-collocation"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Ask, demand, insist, require, recommend — all take the subjunctive.

Why D is wrong The indicative turns the demand into a report of a fact.

stem_html:
The vaccine trial recruited more volunteers in its first month than any previous trial at the centre. ______ nearly a third of them withdrew before the second dose, leaving the final sample smaller than planned.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Therefore,","trap":"transition-reversal"},{"letter":"B","content":"Likewise,","trap":"transition-reversal"},{"letter":"C","content":"For instance,","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"However,"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Good news then bad news is contrast.
  • Ask whether sentence two follows from sentence one.
  • An example must be an instance of the claim.

Why A is wrong Therefore would make the withdrawals a consequence of strong recruitment.

Why B is wrong Likewise claims the two sentences point the same way, and they point opposite ways.

Why C is wrong The second sentence is not an example of the first.

Why D is right A record recruitment followed by a sample smaller than planned is a reversal, which is what however marks.

stem_html:
The alloy resists corrosion in salt water far better than the steel it replaces and costs about the same per tonne. ______ it cannot be welded with the equipment already installed in most yards, which is why adoption has been slow.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Even so,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "As a result,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "In other words,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Moreover,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Advantages then a drawback is a concession.
  • Adding and contrasting are opposite jobs.
  • “Which is why adoption has been slow” marks the drawback.

Why A is right The first sentence lists advantages and the second gives the obstacle that outweighs them, so the transition has to concede and turn.

Why B is wrong The welding problem is not caused by the alloy's cost or corrosion resistance.

Why C is wrong In other words promises a restatement, and the second sentence adds new information.

Why D is wrong Moreover adds another point on the same side, but this point cuts the other way.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Antikythera mechanism is a geared bronze device recovered from a shipwreck in 1901.
  • It models the motions of the sun and moon and predicts eclipses.
  • Nothing of comparable gearing survives from the next thousand years.
  • Scholars disagree about whether it was unique or one of many that were lost.

The student wants to emphasize what remains unsettled about the mechanism. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The mechanism was recovered in 1901 and predicts eclipses.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"Although the mechanism models the sun and moon and predicts eclipses, scholars still disagree about whether it was unique or one of many devices now lost."},{"letter":"C","content":"The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a shipwreck in 1901, is a geared bronze device that models the motions of the sun and moon.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"Nothing of comparable gearing survives from the thousand years after the mechanism was made.","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Unsettled” means find the note that reports a disagreement.
  • A list of facts cannot emphasize an open question.
  • Although sets the known against the unknown in one sentence.

Why A is wrong Two settled facts, and neither touches the open question.

Why B is right The goal is what remains unsettled, and only this choice names the disagreement and sets it against what is known.

Why C is wrong Every clause here is settled fact, so nothing is presented as open.

Why D is wrong The gap in the record is a fact, not the disagreement the goal asks for.
